extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American journalism history; historians and journalism scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Identify quality, editorial, production, legal, and commercial criteria that defined 17th–18th century colonial newspapers (content, appearance, frequency, legal risks, and business practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for a Gazette writer/editor
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Author of a Gazette (in the Opinion of the Learned) ought to be qualified with an extensive Acquaintance with Languages, a great Easiness and Command of Writing and Relating Things clearly and intelligibly, and in a few words; he should be able to speak of War both by Land and Sea; be well acquainted with Geography, with the History of the Time, with the several Interests of Princes and States, the Secrets of Courts, and the Manners and Customs of all Nations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin’s admonition lists the broad learning and rhetorical abilities expected of a newspaper author/editor in the period; the text notes such men were rare in the colonies and that editors should “make up among his Friends what is wanting in himself.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Lively news sense for the unusual and interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong newspaper demonstrates “a lively news sense for the unusual and interesting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Pennsylvania Gazette under Franklin is credited with evidence of a lively news sense; this is presented as an editorial quality that attracts readers and increases a paper’s influence and advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brightness and freedom in treatment of local news
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers may display “brightness and freedom in its treatment of local news.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The American Weekly Mercury is described as sometimes showing more brightness and freedom than contemporaries; this is an evaluative feature distinguishing more engaging local coverage from dry reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness and timeliness of content
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness is a criterion — papers filled with foreign news several months old were criticized (e.g., “chiefly foreign news from three to six months old”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York Gazette’s reliance on stale foreign reports is presented as a weakness compared with papers that handled and selected news more promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of content (literary matter, poetry, essays, serials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful papers and magazines included variety — poetry, belles-lettres, essays, serial stories, and political documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin’s General Magazine gave pages to poetry and belles-lettres; serials (e.g., Defoe’s Religious Courtship, Chambers’s Cyclopaedia entries) were experimented with, but some serials (Keimer’s encyclopedic serial) are criticized as 'irrational' for a newspaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and arrangement of foreign reports and extracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in the selection and arrangement of foreign reports and literary extracts is a mark of editorial ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the Zenger trial the Journal showed 'unusual skill' in arranging foreign reports and literary extracts — this selection/organization is presented as an editorial strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satire, essays, and polemic as editorial tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire and essayistic pieces (e.g., Addisonian essays, Cato’s Letters, word-cartoon paragraphs) were deliberately used to critique rivals or authorities and to attract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the 'Busy-Body' papers used to satirize Keimer, Zenger’s monkey advertisement allegory, and reprinting of Cato’s Letters to support political arguments; such devices could build readership but also provoke libel actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and boldness in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers were evaluated on their willingness to criticize authorities; a 'measure of independence and boldness in criticism' distinguished some editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Weekly Post-Boy and Zenger’s Journal are cited as showing independence and boldness; such editorial stances could lead to arrests, libel accusations, or popular support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risk management: libel law and evidentiary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal standards governing libel shaped journalism: at issue were (a) whether truth could be offered as a defense, and (b) whether a jury had the right to determine if a publication was seditious or defamatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Zenger trial discussion shows competing doctrines: the common-law view that truth did not negate libel versus Hamilton’s argument for admissibility of truth and jury determination. The text notes these principles were not firmly established for many years and that statutory reforms followed later (e.g., Fox Libel Act 1792).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury’s role in libel cases (community judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right and role of the jury to judge whether publications were defamatory or seditious — Hamilton appealed directly to the jury as the community’s judges of truth and character of publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton’s rhetorical appeal to jurors and their subsequent 'not guilty' verdict are presented as a formative moment for press liberty even when the legal doctrines were unsettled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing and typographic quality / handsome appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Production quality — from 'poorly printed' sheets to 'handsomer appearance' — is a marker of a paper’s professionalism and attractiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Keimer’s and early New York papers (poorly printed) with Franklin’s Gazette (handsomer appearance) and the role of better layout and typography in distinguishing a superior newspaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising volume and commercial viability
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of advertising (e.g., requiring six- or eight-page issues at midcentury; five of six pages filled with advertising) indicates commercial success and patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increased advertising both supported larger papers and signaled a paper’s reach and profitability; editors adapted size/frequency to advertising demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency and format (pages, weekly/monthly) as editorial choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Format and frequency (weekly, monthly, biweekly; two to eight pages) are part of a paper’s character and audience reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mercury varied two to four pages; some magazines began as quarterlies or monthlies; frequency and page count affected content mix and advertising capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial networks, patronage, and official positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal ties, partnerships, postmaster appointments, and official printing contracts influenced a paper’s fortunes and distribution (e.g., Franklin’s appointment as postmaster benefitted the Gazette).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin’s encouragement of printers and financial partnerships helped spawn other papers; official roles could confer distributional advantages or patronage income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business practices and partnerships vs. independent chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Early papers sometimes shared owners, partners, or financial backing but remained editorially independent rather than forming formal chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin’s part-ownership and assistance to multiple papers is noted as friendly aid rather than a structured chain; financing and partnerships affected survival and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language newspaper characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-language newspapers (e.g., German 'hoch deutsch' papers) typically catered to ethnic communities and were 'strongly religious in tone.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These papers had different editorial emphases and lifespans; technical capabilities (e.g., Sower’s mechanical skills, paper-mill, type foundry) influenced their sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial continuity and succession (widows, apprentices carrying on)
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers’ businesses and newspapers often passed within families or were carried on by widows or former apprentices; continuity affected survival and editorial direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Andrew Bradford’s widow carried on the Mercury for four years; many women operated presses as printers’ widows; apprentices like Parker and Weyman established successor papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of content to audience and culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of leisure and culture influenced a publication’s viability — e.g., early magazines failed because 'American society did not yet have the leisure or the culture for magazine literature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial planners should match content type and depth (magazine essays, poetry) to audience readiness and subscriber base; subscriber numbers (e.g., a thousand subscribers) determined sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection: avoid irrational or mismatched features (antipattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Including incongruous or overly ambitious features (e.g., serially reprinting an entire encyclopaedia in a newspaper) is criticized as 'irrational' and an editorial antipattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keimer’s Cyclopaedia serial is presented as a poor editorial judgment for a newspaper; editors should prioritize news and reader interest over impractical scholarly serials in that medium.
